spots.name: Shibuya Crossing
spots.label: Shibuya Crossing

text.description:
Shibuya Crossing is the big pedestrian junction outside Shibuya Station, and it is one of the most recognisable street scenes in Tokyo. When the lights turn red for the cars, people cross in every direction at once. The Wikipedia figures put it at roughly 1,000 to 2,000 people on a single green light, and it has been called the world's busiest pedestrian crossing. It opened in 1973 and has appeared in many films, TV shows and music videos, so many visitors already know the view before they arrive.

It photographs well because of the movement and the scale. Crowds, tall buildings and video screens all fit into one frame, and the scene changes with every light cycle. You can take a wide shot of the whole junction or a tighter picture of a few people crossing. The same spot works as a short video clip too.

Standing there gives you a longer view, and the telephoto lens helps you pick out a section of the crowd. Wait for a new green light, because the crowd fills up in the first few seconds. Keep to the pavement and the crossing islands, and do not stop in the road to take a picture. Hold your phone firmly in a busy crowd. Around Halloween and New Year's Eve the area gets very crowded and the local ward has put restrictions in place, so expect rules and tighter security then.
text.directions_text: Start at Shibuya station, which is served by the JR Saikyo Line, JR Shonan-Shinjuku Line, JR Yamanote Line, Tokyo Metro - Denentoshi bypass line, Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line, Tokyo Metro Ginza Line and Tokyo Metro Hanzōmon Line. The crossing is about 174 m to the north-west of the station, about 3 minutes on foot. If you prefer a quieter approach, Meiji-jingumae 'Harajuku' station (Tokyo Metro Chiyoda Line and Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line) is about 1,095 m north of the crossing. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: The crossing is an open public road junction that you can use freely on foot; if you want an elevated view from a building, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Shibuya Crossing is in the Shibuya district of central Tokyo, right outside Shibuya Station, with the crossing lying to the north-west of the station. It sits in a major shopping and entertainment area.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole junction. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from where you stand to bring the crowd and buildings closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to the crossing and want to include the tall buildings and screens.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From there you view the junction from a distance, so use zoom rather than walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals of the buildings straight. Put the crowd on the lower third of the frame and leave room above for the buildings and screens. Take a few shots as each light cycle starts, when the crowd is at its fullest. Try a short Live Photo to catch the flow of people.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the crowd to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little so bright screens don't wash out. In the evening, night mode helps, but hold the phone very still because people are moving. Do not use portrait mode on a distant scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening usually works well, when the video screens and shop lights stand out against the darker sky. Weekday daytimes are often less packed than evenings and weekends. Avoid Halloween and New Year's Eve unless you want the biggest crowds.

spots.name: Tokyo Skytree
spots.label: Tokyo Skytree

text.description:
Tokyo Skytree is a broadcasting and observation tower in Sumida, and at 634 m it is the tallest tower in Japan. It reached that height in early 2011 and opened to the public on 22 May 2012. The number is a word game: 6, 3 and 4 can be read as "Musashi", an old name for the region. The lattice is painted a bluish-white shade called "Skytree White", based on a traditional Japanese colour. The base is a three-legged structure, which gives the tower a distinctive shape from the street.

It photographs well because it is so tall and so clean in outline, with plain sky behind it on a clear day. At night the LED lighting alternates daily between a sky-blue pattern and a purple one, so the tower can look quite different from one evening to the next.

Tall subjects are easiest when you keep the phone upright and level. Tilting it upwards makes the tower lean inwards. Step back to the edge of the open space if you can, and include some foreground, such as a lamp post or a passer-by, to give a sense of height. The observation decks are a separate matter, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go up.
text.directions_text: The closest station is Oshiage (Toei Asakusa Line), about 3 minutes on foot from the phone icon on the map, with the tower to the west. Oshiage (SKYTREE) (Tokyo Metro Hanzōmon Line) is about 4 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 220 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: The tower can be photographed from the surrounding public streets, but the observation decks are a ticketed visit, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Tokyo Skytree stands in Sumida, in the east of Tokyo, about seven km north-east of Tokyo Station. The nearest stations are Oshiage (Toei Asakusa Line) and Oshiage (SKYTREE) (Tokyo Metro Hanzōmon Line), both a short walk to the east of the tower. It is the centerpiece of a large commercial development owned by Tobu Railway.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole tower from this close. The default lens (1x) works for the upper part or a tighter, simpler shot. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the top section against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 220 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. The tower will be straight ahead of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on your gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line to keep it from leaning. Hold the phone upright and level, then raise your arms rather than tilting the phone back. Leave some sky above the tip and add a little foreground at the bottom for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the white lattice does not wash out against bright sky. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body so the lights stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun is behind you in the east and lights the side of the tower facing you. Dusk and after dark are good for the illumination, which alternates daily between sky blue and purple.

text.description:
The Hachikō statue stands in Hachiko Square, right beside Shibuya station. The photo can be as much about the people and the city around it as about the statue. That is why it works well on a phone: you can show the statue small and let the crowds, signs and buildings tell you where you are.

The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. From there the statue is small in the frame. Use it for a scene-setting shot, then walk closer for a tighter picture. The square is often busy, so be patient. Wait a few moments and a gap usually opens up around the statue. Keep to the edge of the walkways so you do not block people heading to the station.

The statue is only about 2 minutes on foot from the station, so it is easy to combine with other stops nearby. Take a wide shot first, then a closer one, and you will have two very different photos in a couple of minutes.
text.directions_text: Head for Shibuya station, served by the JR Saikyo Line, JR Shonan-Shinjuku Line, JR Yamanote Line, Tokyo Metro - Denentoshi bypass line, Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line, Tokyo Metro Ginza Line and Tokyo Metro Hanzōmon Line. The statue is about 123 m to the west of the station, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: The statue is in an open public square beside the station, but check the official site before you go in case of any works or changes.
text.geographic_location: In Shibuya, in Tokyo's Shibuya ward, at Hachiko Square, about 120 m to the west of Shibuya station.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) at the phone icon on the map to show the statue in its square. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a closer view without stepping into the crowd. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are standing close and want the buildings behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. For a closer shot, walk towards the statue along the edge of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the lower thirds, with the square and buildings filling the rest. Wait for a moment when fewer people stand directly in front of it. For a close shot, hold the phone low and level so the statue does not look tilted.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky behind is bright. In a crowd, a Live Photo lets you pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and the evening gives lit signs and a livelier mood. Use night mode after dark and hold the phone steady.
